activities.anchor: occurs at one exact temperature and composition
activities.caption: pair each region of the map with its freedom
activities.name: pdFreedomMatch

config.prompt: The Gibbs phase rule, F = C − P + 1, assigns each region its freedom — pair them:

pairs.right: F = 2 — temperature and composition both vary freely
F = 1 — pick the temperature and both phase compositions are pinned
F = 0 — a single temperature and composition, no freedom left
the ends are fixed by temperature alone; only the proportions follow the overall composition

config.why: That is the geometry behind the whole diagram: pinned endpoints, movable proportions — and the lever rule is just mass balance on the pinned line.

activities.anchor: Solubility limits are where strengthening comes from
activities.caption: drag between the lens and the solvus
activities.name: pdSolubilityCompare

config.prompt: Two ideal behaviours of a binary system — drag between them:

before.label: complete solid solubility
before.text: Cu–Ni: two atoms so alike that one crystal takes any mixture. The diagram is a lens between two melting lines — a single phase field, wall to wall.

after.label: limited solubility
after.text: Most pairs: solid solutions survive only up to a solvus line, beyond which a second phase must appear. Cross that line and precipitates form — the basis of age-hardened aluminium.

config.why: Solubility limits are where strengthening begins: the solvus is the doorway from solid solution to obstacle field.

activities.anchor: no equilibrium diagram of the day
activities.caption: rebuild the discovery that ran ahead of the map
activities.name: pdWilmOrder

config.prompt: Wilm's 1906 observation to modern aircraft skins — drag the story into order:
items: 1906 — a quenched Al–4% Cu alloy keeps strengthening for days at room temperature
Nothing in the equilibrium maps of the era predicts it
1938 — X-ray work reveals tiny copper-rich clusters: Guinier–Preston zones
The quench had trapped a supersaturated solid solution — the solvus crossed in slow motion
The clusters obstruct dislocations far more effectively than the coarse equilibrium phase could
config.why: Age hardening is metallurgy's most valuable piece of non-equilibrium behaviour — the solvus is the only trace it leaves on the equilibrium map.

activities.anchor: In a two-phase region the tie-line is a seesaw
activities.caption: call the carbide fraction of eutectoid steel
activities.name: pdCementiteEstimate

config.prompt: A 0.76% C alloy cools through the eutectoid: ferrite holds 0.022% C, cementite holds 6.7% C. Roughly what fraction of the final pearlite is cementite?
config.why: f(cementite) = (0.76 − 0.022)/(6.7 − 0.022) ≈ 0.11 — about 11% hard carbide in a soft iron matrix. That proportion, and its fineness of dispersion, is most of what the words "steel grade" mean.
config.context: Mass check from the worked example: 0.6 × 70 + 0.4 × 20 = 50 — the seesaw always balances.

activities.anchor: growing cooperatively because each phase rejects
activities.caption: set cast iron's eutectic on the melting scale
activities.name: pdEutecticPlace

config.prompt: Pure iron melts at 1538 °C and solder's eutectic at 183 °C. Place cast iron's 4.3% C eutectic on the scale:
config.why: About 1147 °C — some 390 degrees below pure iron. That gap is why iron could be melted and cast for two millennia before steel could be forged at scale.

activities.caption: file each property with its iron–carbon phase
activities.name: pdFeCBuckets

config.prompt: Three phases carry the iron–carbon story — file each fact:

items.label: BCC iron holding almost no carbon — soft, ductile, magnetic
FCC iron that dissolves up to ~2.1% carbon
exists only at high temperature — heat steel and the carbon vanishes into solution
a brittle iron-carbide compound at 6.7% C
extremely hard — provides much of steel's strength

config.why: Steel lives in the narrow corridor between ferrite's refusal of carbon and cementite's 6.7% excess — and the eutectoid sandwich between them is pearlite.

activities.anchor: the lever rule drawn in volts
activities.caption: which voltage curve is the two-phase cathode?
activities.name: pdPlateauTrace

config.prompt: State of charge on x, cell voltage on y — which trace is the two-phase LiFePO₄-style cathode?
config.why: In a two-phase field the phase rule pins lithium's chemical potential — and a pinned potential is a flat plateau (~3.45 V). Curve A is the solid-solution glide of an NMC cathode: no plateau, but composition readable from voltage.

activities.anchor: moves perhaps a hundredth of a volt
activities.caption: walk the fuel-gauge decision
activities.name: pdGaugeBranch

config.root: Your device must report remaining charge, and the only sensor is voltage. Choose the chemistry.

start.text: Three electrode chemistries are on the table. Which do you build the gauge around?

choices.label: LiFePO₄ — the famously flat ~3.45 V plateau
choices.feedback: Superbly stable voltage — and nearly mute as a gauge.

choices.label: Layered NMC — a continuous solid solution
choices.feedback: Voltage glides as lithium leaves: composition readable from voltage.

choices.label: Graphite anode — discrete stage compounds
choices.feedback: A staircase of small plateaus, not a slope.

flat.text: Two phases coexist, the phase rule pins the chemical potential, and voltage barely moves from empty to full. The gauge must count coulombs instead — the voltmeter is reading the map, not the tank.

glide.text: A continuous solid solution has a composition-dependent chemical potential, so voltage tracks lithium content directly. The trade: none of the plateau's stability, all of the readability.

stage.text: Lithium fills every nth gallery between graphene sheets, down to fully stoichiometric LiC₆ near 0.1 V — the gauge sees steps between stages, each a small two-phase field of its own.

config.why: Voltage is a chemical-potential difference — whether it sits flat, glides or steps is the electrode's phase diagram showing through.
